name: Whiteboard
basis: why: one line width, a few colours, strokes that run dry; how: even outlines, streaky fills, ghost ink, glare

lumenary.blurb: A dry-wipe marker drawing: even black outlines, shadows filled with streaky strokes in blue, red and green, the ghost of last week’s notes and glare across the board.

why: A marker has one line width and a handful of colours. Whoever draws with it works fast, outlines the shapes, and fills dark areas with a few diagonal strokes that run dry before the end. The board itself is glossy, so there is glare, and it is never quite clean. The result is a drawing that explains something, which is what a whiteboard is for.
how: Paint the board: near white, glare across it, faint smears of old ink.
Blur the picture well and outline its shapes at one even width.
Fill the dark areas with slanted strokes separated by gaps.
Let each stroke run dry, and cross the strokes in the darkest areas.
Pick black, red, green or blue for each area from the picture’s colour.
Add the aluminium frame, the tray, the markers and the eraser.
history: Enamelled steel boards that could be written on and wiped were sold from the 1960s, but they needed a damp cloth. The dry-wipe marker, whose ink sits on the surface and brushes off, arrived in the mid 1970s. Offices adopted the whiteboard first, and during the 1990s it replaced the chalkboard in many schools, partly to keep chalk dust away from computers.
terms: Ink that dries as a film on a smooth board and rubs off without water.
How far a colour is from grey.
Faint traces of old writing left on a board after erasing.
paragraphs: The board is almost white: slightly grey toward the corners, crossed by a soft band of glare shaped like a bell curve, and tinted in places by smears of ink that were never quite wiped off. Those ghost marks are two fractal noises, each stretched hard in one direction and cut at a threshold. Outlines are found on a copy of the picture blurred twice, because a marker cannot draw hair, only shapes. The edge strength is cut at a threshold divided by the tip size, so a broader tip simply accepts weaker edges and the line fattens.

Shading is done in strokes. The position of a pixel across the stroke direction, divided by the stroke spacing, says whether it lies in a stroke or in the gap between two. A stroke is drawn only where the picture is dark enough, and a slow noise along its length makes it run dry and stop. The darkest areas get a second set of strokes across the first. Colour is chosen per pixel from the smoothed picture: black when the colour is dull or very dark, otherwise red, green or blue by hue. A colour has to be clearly a colour to earn a coloured marker.

equations.note: The band of light across the board; u and v are the position from 0 to 1.
Outline from the edge strength E of the blurred picture; τ is the tip size.

equations.tex: \text{marker}=\begin{cases}\text{black}&\max(R,G,B)-\min(R,G,B)<62\ \text{or}\ D>0.86\\ \text{red, green or blue}&\text{by hue otherwise}\end{cases}
equations.note: Choice of marker from the smoothed colour; D is the darkness of the picture.

presets.text: Black only with a fine tip looks like a careful diagram.
A fat tip and little detail give a bold doodle.
Heavy ghost marks make a board nobody cleaned.
